comparison: Both strongly support the methodology claims (C2, C16-C27, C95-C98). OpenEval emphasizes comprehensive methodological details and quantitative results. Peer reviewers explicitly praised it as 'a gold standard in antibody validation' and 'a major achievement.' High agreement on methodological rigor.

Both address C43 regarding correlations between IF success and other applications. OpenEval finds the claim SUPPORTED by statistical analysis (McNemar test). Peer reviewer finds it UNCERTAIN and 'surprising,' questioning why IP and WB have similar predictive value for IF when IP should theoretically be more predictive. Significant disagreement on interpretation.

Both address manufacturer responses (C7, C57). OpenEval rates SUPPORTED, noting concrete actions (73 withdrawn, 153 modified). Peer reviewers also SUPPORTED, treating it as a positive outcome and endorsing the initiative's impact. Strong agreement.

Both address bibliometric data on underperforming antibodies in literature (C58-C63, C6, C67). OpenEval rates UNCERTAIN due to concerns about generalizability of the 65-protein sample. Peer reviewers rate SUPPORTED, explicitly acknowledging it as 'a worrying aspect' without challenging the extrapolation to 20-30% of literature figures. Moderate disagreement on certainty level.

Both address data dissemination (C64, C26, C27). OpenEval rates SUPPORTED, praising the well-designed data sharing strategy. Peer reviewers rate UNCERTAIN, acknowledging the open data approach but identifying significant usability limitations requiring a searchable database. Disagreement on implementation adequacy.

Both address impact claims (C65, C66, C94). OpenEval rates SUPPORTED with appropriate qualification that long-term impact remains to be demonstrated. Peer reviewers strongly SUPPORTED, calling it 'a landmark effort' that 'will ensure researchers only use well-validated antibodies.' Strong agreement with peer reviewers more emphatic.

Both address cost and scalability (C11, C12, C68-C71). OpenEval rates SUPPORTED, treating cost estimates as reasonable order-of-magnitude projections. Peer reviewers rate UNCERTAIN, explicitly questioning scalability and stating 'the feasibility of testing hundreds of thousands of antibodies on the market should be discussed in more detail.' Disagreement on adequacy of cost-benefit justification.

Both address antibody types and recombinant recommendations (C81-C87, C90). OpenEval rates SUPPORTED, finding the recommendation logically follows from performance data. Peer reviewers also SUPPORTED without challenge, though one reviewer's concern about confounding (in R4) suggests the recommendation's strength may depend on resolving that uncertainty. General agreement.

Both address KO-based validation recommendations and biobank proposal (C91-C93, C11). OpenEval rates SUPPORTED as logical recommendations. Peer reviewers also SUPPORTED, unanimously endorsing the KO-based methodology as 'gold standard' and implicitly supporting the biobank recommendation. Strong agreement.

Both address recombinant antibody superiority (C37-C41, C5, C89). OpenEval rates SUPPORTED with appropriate caution about C42 (possible confounding). Peer reviewers rate UNCERTAIN, raising the same critical question about whether superior performance reflects differential pre-validation rather than inherent superiority. Agreement on the need for caution, but different certainty ratings.

Both address validation method comparisons (C50-C56, with overlap on C44-C49). OpenEval rates SUPPORTED, finding genetic strategies more reliable than orthogonal approaches. Peer reviewers also SUPPORTED, implicitly accepting by praising the knockout-based methodology as 'gold standard.' Strong agreement.

Both address protein sample characterization and extrapolation (C72-C80, C32). OpenEval rates SUPPORTED with appropriate qualification of extrapolation as speculative. Peer reviewers also SUPPORTED, noting the 'encouraging result' and implicitly endorsing extrapolation validity. Strong agreement.

Both address background context and problem characterization (C1, C8-C10, C28-C31). OpenEval rates SUPPORTED, noting proper citations to peer-reviewed literature. Peer reviewers also SUPPORTED, accepting claims without challenge and endorsing the characterization of the reproducibility problem. Strong agreement.

Both address failure rates and validation outcomes (C44-C49, C3). OpenEval rates SUPPORTED with systematic comparison data. Peer reviewers also SUPPORTED, acknowledging failure rates without challenge and treating them as accepted findings, with one calling the high IF failure rate 'a worrying aspect.' Strong agreement.

Both address database analysis and Antibody Registry data (C28-C31). OpenEval rates SUPPORTED, noting proper citation and consistency. Peer reviewers also SUPPORTED as part of background claims accepted without challenge. Strong agreement.

Both address experimental coverage data (C32-C36, with peer R3 including C33-C36). OpenEval rates SUPPORTED with quantitative reporting. Peer reviewers also SUPPORTED, explicitly endorsing coverage findings as 'a major achievement' and 'an encouraging result.' Strong agreement.

Both address C42 regarding possible confounding in recombinant antibody performance. OpenEval rates SUPPORTED, noting the authors appropriately show scientific caution. Peer reviewers also SUPPORTED, with one reviewer independently raising the same concern, validating it as a legitimate alternative explanation. Strong agreement on the importance of this caveat.

OpenEval R14 addresses C13 (study partnership composition and 27% market share), rating it SUPPORTED as a verifiable factual claim. No corresponding peer review result specifically evaluates this claim, though peer R1 includes C13 in its claim set without specific commentary on market share representation.
